title: Advancing training effectiveness prediction in mass sport through longitudinal data: a mathematical model approach based on the Fitness-Fatigue Model
authors: Wang W, Zhao Y, Hou X, Yu W, Ren H, Ren H
population: 13 recreational subjects, 12 weeks of medium-intensity continuous cycling, 28-42 days of daily data per person (420 paired data points)
findings: External load (speed, wattage) and wearable-compatible internal indicators (HRV and heart rate recovery related) were collected on each training day and the model was fitted and evaluated for each individual separately.
With the optimal output indicator selected, the optimised model had R2 0.61-0.95, fitting RMSE 0.07-0.37 and predictive MAPE 3.99%-31.99%.
With an inappropriate output indicator some individuals had minimum R2 0.32, maximum RMSE 0.90 and maximum MAPE 86.57%.
Optimal indicator selection varies by individual; HRV and HRR related indicators are proposed as generalisable model outputs usable through wearables.
limitations: 13 homogeneous cycling subjects, one training type, short duration; predictive error is highly variable. The model output is a physiological indicator (HRV/HRR), not race or time-trial performance, so it is a weak proxy for the performance target. The paper's modified model is not fully specified in the abstract.
implications: If wearable HRV/HRR is used as a response variable, select the output indicator per athlete by forward validation and fall back to load-only guidance when predictive error is high.
Expect noisy daily recovery signals; smooth them before fitting.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, PLOS One, 2025-12-03. Numbers match Europe PMC abstract. Added caveat that the outcome is a physiological proxy rather than performance.
